I do not have a patient temperament and therefore would not make a good teacher (as a profession). However, I am the only available "tech support" and there are some times when they have to use the computer. So I'm trying to use concrete "old tech" metaphors to explain "new tech" concepts to the 'rents but they're not getting it.

Like just now my father has to type something for his job that's on a provided "template" which already has material in it he wants to keep. So he kind of gets the idea of Save (except that he can never find what he was working on again and there's now 40 Word documents on the desktop), but Save As is Chinese rocket surgery for some reason. I tried to explain that it's like having two "Xerox copies" of the same paper document, but you only write on copy 2. Copy 1 doesn't get any pen markings if you write on copy 2. I even took two pieces of blank paper and wrote only on one of them to point out that the original copy remains intact.

I had to clear a paper jam from hell the other day because dad loaded notebook paper into the printer instead of printer paper, despite the fact that I specifically indicated the type of paper to use. He doesn't get that not all papers are created equal and that even though you, a person, can write with a pen on printer paper, the printer has a fit if someone tries to print a document on lined notebook paper. Especially since he remembers typing on a notebook page with a typewriter.

So that's where the aforementioned paper metaphor (for Save As) falls apart -- because it literally involves paper and is thus confusing somehow.

My mother, meanwhile, is even more old-fashioned and would try to operate the computer with a TV remote. No, we don't have one of those Smart TVs and never had Microsoft Web TV. It's just regular Comcast cable and we're using an HP desktop with the standard keyboard and mouse. Obviously the monitor looks like a TV, so she thinks that if she aims the remote at the monitor it'll turn on. I then have to show her again that you have to push the power button. She has since given up on the whole concept and walked away frustrated and shouting F-bombs up the basement stairs. This is extremely unlike her, BTW: she hates cursing and won't even call drivers who cut her off assholes -- she prefers childlike terms like "stinky face" and "silly goose" and "tuna fish" (tuna fish?), which do sound kind of odd for someone who is in their middle 50s by now.

My father doesn't have that luxury of giving up, because he works and has to use the computer for certain aspects of his job, while she's a stay-at-home and doesn't really "have to" learn any more about it. He's also the oldest employee and is getting fed up with the younger workers who snicker when he calls copy and paste "scratch and sniff." I therefore don't have the luxury of fully giving up, because if he isn't able to use the computer he's SOL, and we're all out on the street because his retirement got wiped out in 2007 by the unscrupulous hedge-fund assholes (sorry, tuna fish). So I'm at my wits' end having to explain that Save As doesn't mean "save your ass," that a printer is not a typewriter, and that sending someone an e-mail doesn't necessarily mean you print out the email and put it in an envelope with a stamp.

Anyone else go through wrist-slitting frustration trying to teach old folks the computer? How did 70-year-old Trump learn Twitter when I can't even get my folks, ~15-20 years younger, to understand that "it's on the desktop" doesn't literally mean somewhere on the table?
